title: EditLens: Quantifying the Extent of AI Editing in Text
claim: Edits fall on a continuous spectrum between fully human and fully AI text, and an edit's distance from the original measures its magnitude.
layout: 5 cards in a tree: 2 endpoints on top, 3 edits below, distance badges
description: Five rounded cards show one text about driverless cars at different levels of AI involvement. The top row has a green 'Fully Human' card with a typo-ridden sentence, scored 0.00, and a red 'Fully AI Generated' card, scored 1.00. A purple connector links them to three cards in the bottom row, each with a human+robot icon and a quoted edit prompt: 'Fix any mistakes' (0.07), 'Sound Fluent' (0.29) and 'Make it more descriptive' (0.36). Text fragments are highlighted in cyan, pink and lavender, so the same ideas can be traced across versions. The highlights show minor fixes staying close to the original while heavier edits rewrite it. Rounded pill badges in each card's lower-right corner give the cosine distance. The eye goes first to the colored headers at the top, then down to the increasing scores.
caption: AI edits exist on a continuous spectrum from fully human written to fully AI generated. Here we show three versions of the same human-written text after different edits have been applied by an LLM alongside the cosine distance between the edited text and the fully human text. Texts have been truncated for space. "Fix any mistakes," the most mild edit according to cosine distance, results in a text with only spelling and grammar errors corrected, while "Make it more descriptive" closely adheres to the ideas in the human-written text while substantially rewriting it.
abstract: A significant proportion of queries to large language models ask them to edit user-provided text, rather than generate new text from scratch. While previous work focuses on detecting fully AI-generated text, we demonstrate that AI-edited text is distinguishable from human-written and AI-generated text. First, we propose using lightweight similarity metrics to quantify the magnitude of AI editing present in a text given the original human-written text and validate these metrics with human annotators. Using these similarity metrics as intermediate supervision, we then train EditLens, a regression model that predicts the amount of AI editing present within a text. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on both binary (F1=94.7%) and ternary (F1=90.4%) classification tasks in distinguishing human, AI, and mixed writing. Not only do we show that AI-edited text can be detected, but also that the degree of change made by AI to human writing can be detected, which has implications for authorship attribution, education, and policy. Finally, as a case study, we use our model to analyze the effects of AI-edits applied by Grammarly, a popular writing assistance tool. To encourage further research, we commit to publicly releasing our models and dataset.
